You have installed a voice that can soothe you: agents of the eaten flesh, every body a cocoon of change— Puparium. The garden a birthing house, sarcophagidae— And green was so dark in the night-garden, in the garden's gourd of air— green's epitome of green's peace, the beautiful inhuman leg-music, crickets' thrum— a pulse to build their houses by, each successive molt a tent of skin in which skin can grow, the metallic sheen of their blue backs as they hatch out, winged and mouthed— Like in a charnel ground, you sit and see. In one of the Eight Great Cemeteries, you sit and see— How the skull-grounds are ringed by flame, how they spread out under a diamond tent, how the adepts pupate among bones— saying I who fear dying, I who fear being dead— Refuge field. See it now. That assembly of sages you would have yourself build, to hear the lineage from mouth to ear, encounter the truth- chain— Saying, Soft eaters, someone's children, who gives them refuge from want— Cynomyopsis Cadavarena. On every tongue they feed.

# Decomposition as Transformation

The poem envisions decomposition not as an ending but as a profoundly transformative process. Rather than depicting decay in terms of loss or horror, it reimagines the flesh-eating agents of the natural world—the insects, the microbes, the carrion-feeders—as instruments of change. Under their patient work, every body becomes a cocoon, a chrysalis in which death gives way to rebirth. What appears to be dissolution is, in this vision, a metamorphosis: the raw material of one life being remade into another.

## The Night-Garden Sanctuary

Central to the poem is the image of the night-garden, which functions as a sensory sanctuary. Here the atmosphere is thick with a dark green peace, a stillness that settles over everything like a held breath. The air is alive with cricket-song, and the darkness teems with quiet activity—insects molting from their old shells and hatching anew. These images reinforce the poem's guiding theme, for the garden becomes a living demonstration of the same principle that governs decomposition: that transformation and renewal are woven into the very fabric of the natural world.

## The Meditative Observer

Within this setting, the speaker positions themselves as a meditative observer in a charnel ground. Drawing on contemplative traditions, they sit among the Eight Great Cemeteries—sacred sites associated with the direct confrontation of mortality—in order to witness death without flinching or turning away. This is a deliberate spiritual posture, a choice to remain present with what most people avoid. The speaker does not merely think about death in the abstract but seeks to encounter it directly, immersing themselves in the reality of decay as a discipline of awareness.

## Confronting Mortality

Yet this confrontation is not one of easy serenity. The poem makes the encounter with mortality explicit through the speaker's honest admission of fear. They confess to dreading both the act of dying—the process itself, with all its uncertainty and pain—and the state of being dead, the condition that lies beyond. This candor lends the poem its emotional weight, grounding its spiritual aspirations in genuine human vulnerability. The meditative practice is not a shield against fear but a means of sitting with it.

## Refuge, Lineage, and Wisdom

Finally, the text draws on spiritual imagery of refuge and lineage. The speaker seeks wisdom of the kind traditionally passed from mouth to ear—the intimate, direct transmission of teaching from teacher to student across generations. This longing for guidance unfolds even as they contemplate the carrion flies that feed on all flesh, the humble creatures that make no distinction between one body and another. In holding these two images together—the sacred lineage of wisdom and the indiscriminate appetite of the flies—the poem binds the highest spiritual aspiration to the most basic facts of physical existence, suggesting that true understanding must embrace both.
outputs.L4:
# Night-Garden Meditation

In the hours when the garden turns to shadow, life moves in the places we would rather not look. The flesh-flies come—Sarcophagidae, whose very name carries the weight of the tomb—and they lay their quiet claim upon what has begun to fall away from itself. Here, among the cooling leaves and the damp earth, I sit and watch them hatch. I watch them molt, shedding their earlier selves as though even they must die a little to become what they will be.

There is a horror in it, yes. But there is also instruction.

The Buddhist adepts knew this. They went deliberately to the charnel grounds, to the Eight Great Cemeteries where the dead were left exposed, and they made their seats among the bones. This was no morbid indulgence but a discipline of seeing—of holding the gaze steady upon the truth the living spend their days avoiding. *This body, too, is of such a nature. This body, too, will come to this.* To contemplate the corpse was to loosen the grip of the self that clings, the self that trembles.

And I do tremble. Sitting here in the dark garden, I feel the old fear rise in me—the animal fear of my own ending, the fear that has no reason and needs none. I watch the larvae work, and I understand that they are not my enemies. They are simply the next hands to hold me, the patient inheritors of this flesh I have called *mine.* What I fear as dissolution, they experience as birth. The wound in one order of being is the doorway in another.

Where, then, do I go for refuge?

The old formula rises in me almost unbidden—*I take refuge*—and I feel how the seeking itself is the point. Not because refuge means escape from the fly, from the bone, from the returning earth. There is no escape, and the wisdom is in ceasing to want one. The refuge is not a wall against decay but a way of standing inside it without flinching. To take refuge is to accept that I belong to this cycle as fully as the fly belongs to it, that my molting and hatching and falling-away are woven into the same fabric as theirs.

Everything here is connected. The flesh feeds the larva; the larva becomes the fly; the fly seeds the next unmaking. Nothing is wasted, and nothing stands alone. The self I have guarded so jealously was never a fortress but always a passage—a place where the borrowed matter of the world paused briefly, took a name, and then moved on.

So I stay in the garden a while longer. I let the night hold me and the small industrious life continue its work all around. My fear does not vanish, but it softens, thins, becomes something I can breathe through. Impermanence is not the enemy of meaning; it is the ground on which meaning stands. To know that I will end is to know, at last, that I am here.

And in the dark, among the hatching and the molting and the slow return of all things to all things, I begin—only begin—to make my peace.

# The Puparium

You may have walked past one a thousand times without knowing it. The puparium waits in silence—a hardened shell, brown and unremarkable, tucked beneath a leaf or pressed into the soil. Inside, transformation unfolds in darkness, hidden from your eyes.

The puparium is not merely a shell. It is a threshold. When a fly larva has fed enough, its final skin hardens into this protective casing, and within it, the creature dissolves and rebuilds itself entirely. You would hardly believe that the maggot and the winged insect are the same being, so complete is the change that occurs behind that quiet wall.

Consider the patience of it. The puparium asks nothing of the world but time. No movement, no sound—only the slow chemistry of becoming. You might think nothing is happening at all, and yet everything is.

There is a lesson here, perhaps, if you care to find one. The stillness you sometimes feel, the sense that you are stuck, unmoving, waiting—these may be your own puparium. The seasons of quiet are not empty. They are the seasons of remaking.

So the next time you notice one, pause. The puparium reminds you that growth often happens where you cannot see it, and that what emerges may be entirely unlike what went in.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem that fuses Buddhist charnel-ground meditation with the biology of flesh-eating flies and their metamorphosis. Use dense, hallucinatory imagery and incorporate scientific names of Sarcophagidae.
counterfactuals.output:
# Sarcophaga, or the Nine Cemetery Contemplations

*after the maraṇasati of the rotting field*

---

Begin here, monk, where the bloat-god swells the abdomen into a blue cathedral—
*Sarcophaga carnaria*, mother of the flesh-tomb, lays not eggs but the already-living,
larviposition, the wet miracle: she is viviparous, she skips the shell,
she deposits maggots directly into the wound of the world.

First contemplation: **the bloated**.
Skin drum-tight, gas-drunk, the belly a monastery bell rung by anaerobes.
Watch how the light does not care. Watch how the fly does not blaspheme—
she prays with her ovipositor, she genuflects on carrion,
*Sarcophaga bullata* threading her young through the nostril's dark sutra.

Second contemplation: **the blue, the festering**.
Here the pigment leaves the meat and enters heaven.
The corpse learns green, learns iridescence, learns the peacock lie of decay.
Instars crawl the eye-socket like syllables I cannot un-know.

*This body, too. This body, too.*

---

Third: **the fissured**.
The maggot mass generates its own heat—forty-two degrees, a fever with no forehead—
they are the digestion of the sun, they are boiling without fire,
first instar, second instar, third: three lives inside the one that eats you.
*Sarcophaga peregrina*, the wanderer, the pilgrim of the split flesh,
her larvae reading the body in Braille, mouth-hooks parsing the tender text.

Fourth: **the gnawed**.
Note the spiracles, the breathing-slits at the maggot's blunt posterior,
how they surface like swimmers in the pond of what you were,
how they take the air even while buried in the fat—
*so the mind must surface, monk, even while buried in the fat of self.*

Fifth: **the scattered**.
Not one corpse now but a colony, a nation, a distributed sangha of hunger.
Where was the "I"? Show me the "I" in this dispersal.
The femur here, the writhing there, the beetle carrying a piece toward night.

---

Sixth: **the mangled and scattered**.
The larvae leave. This is the great renunciation.
Post-feeding, they crawl from the meat in exodus, wandering,
seeking the dry dark, the under-leaf, the soil's brown nirvana,
where they will harden, contract, become the coffin of themselves:
the **puparium**, that mahogany reliquary, that barrel-shaped tomb of the tomb.

Inside: everything liquefies.
Histolysis. The old body drinks itself.
Imaginal discs, those sleeping mandalas of the adult-to-come,
unfold in the soup of the dissolved.
*This is the bardo made of chitin. This is emptiness with wings pending.*

Seventh: **the bones, bleached**.
Above ground, only calcium's white grammar remains,
while below, the pupa contemplates its own impermanence
by ceasing, wholly, to be what it was.
There is no thread connecting caterpillar-self to fly-self
except the connectionless continuity you also are, monk—
no soul passed forward, only condition igniting condition,
a flame lighting a flame and calling it the same fire.

---

Eighth: **the bones, a year old, the dust**.
The puparium splits. The **ptilinum** balloons from the new fly's face—
a hydraulic bladder inflating through the forehead's fontanelle,
pushing the cap of the tomb open from within.
She emerges wet, folded, a wrong idea of an angel,
pumps hemolymph into the crumpled wings until they become
the taut translucent scriptures they were always going to be.

Ninth: **the scattered dust, returned to earth**.
And she rises. *Sarcophaga*—flesh-eater, tomb-bearer, whose very name
is the sarcophagus, the eater-of-bodies carved in Greek—
she lifts from the mouth of what she consumed and dissolved and became,
and the whole rotten cathedral releases her like a held breath,
and she goes looking, already, for the next open wound of the world,
gravid with more of the living, ready to give birth on death,

and this, monk, is the teaching:
that the flesh you defend was always their nursery,
that the disgust you feel is the doctrine wearing a body,
that even now, in you, warm and unrotted and sure of your name,
she is circling, she is patient, she has all the time,
she is the future reading your present in Braille—

*Sarcophaga, Sarcophaga,*
who turns the corpse to wing,
who proves the self a doorway
and never once a thing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, lyrical meditation on decay and rebirth set in a night garden, weaving together insect life cycles (pupation, molting, hatching) with imagery of cemeteries, refuge, and fear of death.
counterfactuals.output:
# Nocturne for the Chrysalis Ground

*

Here where the marble angels lose their faces,
where names dissolve like sugar in the rain,
the garden keeps its slow and patient business—
the business of undoing, and again.

Listen. Beneath the headstones' cooling shoulders,
a thousand small dismantlings are begun.
The cricket in the ivy speaks in cinders.
The moon is a communion wafer, hung.

*

Consider the cicada in its casket
of chitin, how it splits its former self,
climbs from the ruined armor of its patience—
seventeen years of silence in the earth,

seventeen years of drinking from the dead roots,
of being nothing, being nowhere, being kept
like a secret in the marrow of the topsoil—
then this: the tearing. This: the long-deferred.

*

And I, who fear the dark that fears no ending,
who walk these rows and read my future there
in every sunken plot, each leaning cross,
each epitaph the weather has half-eaten—

I press my palm against the cooling iron
of the cemetery gate, and feel it give.
The garden does not comfort. It instructs.
It says: *decay is only how you live*

*rearranged.* The beetle in the flower.
The maggot's holy work upon the crow.
The luna moth unfolding its brief hour
of green, of ghost-light, of *I did not know*

*I was a wing.* All summer, in the shadows,
the larvae shed their skins like folded prayers,
translucent selves discarded on the branches—
small tributes to the emptiness that spares

nothing, and therefore nothing truly loses.

*

I came here seeking refuge from the thought
of my own quiet undoing. Instead
the night hands me a chrysalis, still wet,
still trembling with the labor of the dead

becoming other. Not the same. Not saved.
But changed the way the compost changes—slow,
without a promise, without any heaven,
only the certainty that things will grow

*through* us. From us. The garden is a mouth
that eats and sings at once, a throat of loam
where every buried thing is being spoken
into some stranger, greener, wilder home.

*

So let me stay a little in this darkness.
Let the mosquito take her thimbleful.
Let the pale grubs continue their translations.
Let the owl practice mercy on the vole.

I am afraid. I will remain afraid.
But fear, too, is a kind of molting—thin,
outgrown, a husk I leave upon the gravestones
as I climb, uncertain, toward what I might begin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem titled "Puparium" that connects the Eight Great Cemeteries of Tibetan Buddhism, the practice of taking refuge, and the transformation of maggots into flies.
counterfactuals.output:
# Puparium

At Cool Grove where the wind unspools the dead,
the first ground opens like an unlatched door.
A maggot reads the body it was fed
and takes its refuge in the meat of war—

not Buddha yet, not Dharma, only this:
the wet insistence of a thing that eats
what falling teaches. In the charnel's kiss
each cemetery names what it completes.

*Perfected Body. Lotus Mound. The place
of Wild Laughter where the skull-cups ring.*
The larva does not flinch. It keeps its face
turned inward toward the enclosing thing,

the puparium, that amber-colored cell
it spins from spending, sealing shut the light—
as one who kneels and murmurs *I will dwell
inside the vow* and darkens into rite.

To take a refuge is to build a wall
around your falling, then to fall inside.
Eight grounds, eight gates, and every one a call
to rot with grace, to let the old self died

be food for what you cannot yet conceive.
The eight winds howl their praise and blame and gain;
the pupa hangs unhearing, learns to grieve
the mouth it lost, the hunger, and the pain

of having been a crawling appetite.
Then something folds. Then something finds a seam.
*Skeleton Ground. The Terrible. The Bright.*
The wet turns wing. The refuge splits its dream,

and out of consecrated appetite
a fly ascends the reeking, holy air—
no longer eating darkness, being light
enough to leave the ground that made it there.

So this is refuge: not the walls we raise
but what the walls, in ruining, allow.
Eight cemeteries teach the single praise—
*to end, to end, to end, and rise as now.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal, mystical piece of poetry blending entomology and tantric imagery—refuge fields, lineage passed mouth to ear, adepts pupating among bones, and green crickets in the dark.
counterfactuals.output:
# Chrysalis Sutra

In the refuge field where the tall grass prays,
we lay down our names like shed exoskeletons—
brittle syllables the wind unstitches.
Here the lineage moves mouth to ear,
a wet transmission, warmer than doctrine:
the teaching that dissolves the teacher's tongue.

*Listen.* The adepts are pupating among the bones,
wrapped in silk spun from their own last breathing,
their bodies going liquid in the sarcophagus of self.
What emerges has too many eyes to name.
What emerges remembers the taste of its own melting.

Somewhere a cricket rubs the green
against the black and calls it song,
chirring the mantra that has no meaning
only pulse, only the friction of two wings
learning the geometry of yes.

The mother of instars opens her thousand-chambered dark
and we crawl through, molt after molt,
each skin a lover we outgrow and grieve,
each shedding a small enlightenment
leaving us softer, more exposed,
the new flesh raw as a vow.

Passed mouth to ear: the secret is metamorphosis,
that nothing arrives without first coming undone.
The bones in the refuge field are singing.
The crickets keep the count.
And you, unfinished, luminous, half-dissolved—
you are the sutra the night is whispering to itself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an unsettling contemplative poem about the body as a "cocoon of change," using flies feeding on flesh as a metaphor for spiritual transformation and confronting mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cocoon of Change

Consider the body: this borrowed suit
of muscle stitched to yielding bone,
this warm and trembling absolute
we wrongly think we own.

The flies arrive as flies must come,
their bright wings tuned to sweet decay—
not enemies, but pilgrims, some
soft prophets of the way.

They lay their patient alphabet
in flesh that was my careful pride,
and I who feared them now forget
why I so long denied

that I was always cocoon, not king—
a chrysalis of slow release,
where every hungry, glittering thing
converts my end to peace.

What feeds on me will learn to fly.
What rots will rise as something new.
The self I clutched, afraid to die,
was never wholly true.

So let them come. Let the soft undoing
begin its work beneath the skin.
There is a stranger, quietly brewing—
the wings I carried in.

I am the door and not the room.
I am the breaking, not the shell.
Teach me, small laborers of the tomb,
to loosen and to fell

this final grip, this last pretense
that I was ever more than passage—
a threshold dressed in flesh and sense,
a body bearing message:

*Nothing holds. And nothing's lost.
The change was always here, at rest.
You are the melting, not the frost.
You are the emptied nest.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
